episodes.title: CaLLM: Continual Adaptation of LLMs via Non-Parametric Adapter Routing
episodes.headline: Route incoming tasks without retraining the router
episodes.description: A frozen prompt representation selects lightweight adapters for supervised continual fine-tuning.
episodes.takeaway: Separate routing errors from forgetting within individual experts.
episodes.caveat: Capacity limits can overwrite old experts; dialogue fine-tuning does not outperform the untouched backbone, and online results lack multi-seed uncertainty.
episodes.source_credit:
arXiv:2610.36994v1 · 27 Oct 2026
https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.36994v1
arXiv v1; primary PDF/comments report CoLLAs 2026 acceptance; independent proceedings not located
Original CaLLM Figure 1 and Table 1 excerpts: Celik, Vettoruzzo and Vanschoren, CC BY 4.0 https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/ . Cropping/rearrangement disclosed. Other panels are explanatory adaptations.
episodes.transcript:
CaLLM: Continual Adaptation of LLMs via Non-Parametric Adapter Routing
First publication: 2026-10-27 | Version: v1 (2026-10-27)
Video produced: 2026-11-01 | Selection digest: 2026-10-30
Publication status: arXiv preprint; peer review not independently verified.
Primary source: https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.36994v1

A language model that learns code today should not forget yesterday's science questions. Sequentially updating one small trainable module can still overwrite earlier skills. This paper asks whether a frozen base model can route incoming data into separate lightweight modules, preserving incompatible skills while letting similar tasks share capacity. The challenge is deciding which module to use without being handed a task identifier.

Replay stores old examples and mixes them into later training. Weight penalties discourage changes deemed important to previous tasks. Parameter isolation instead protects old modules, but requires a reliable selection mechanism. Here the system compares distributions of prompts, not just task names. If its fixed representation fails to distinguish two domains, their updates can still collide. Bounded capacity also means an old expert may eventually be overwritten.

The demonstrated setting is supervised continual fine-tuning, not autonomous online learning from unlabeled experience. TRACE-eight is a benchmark of eight diverse language, code and reasoning tasks. A second benchmark contains nineteen dialogue tasks, augmented here with three thousand synthetic examples per task. All methods use the same four-bit Gemma three twelve-billion-parameter backbone. Scores mix task-specific metrics, so a normalized average is not ordinary accuracy.

For each incoming batch, the frozen language model averages token features into a single vector. The router compares that vector with stored prototype vectors using cosine distance. A close match reuses an adapter, meaning a small low-rank weight update added to the frozen model. A novel batch creates one if space remains; otherwise the least-used slot is repurposed. Training changes only the selected adapter using target-token prediction loss. The reused prototype becomes the average of its old value and the new batch vector. At evaluation, routing selects the nearest prototype without modifying memory.

In Table one, after the eight-task sequence, the normalized average is zero point four one for CaLLM, versus zero point three nine for TreeLoRA and zero point two nine for the untouched backbone. Science question accuracy is eighty-one percent versus seventy-two for TreeLoRA. But arithmetic accuracy favors TreeLoRA, and fine-tuning the dialogue benchmark never beats the untouched backbone. These are author-reported comparisons, not an independent state-of-the-art ranking. The paper's prose reports a different aggregate from its table, so these numbers follow the table.

The reusable idea is to keep the routing representation fixed while learning modular expertise. It offers a clean experiment for continual memory: measure routing errors separately from forgetting within experts. However, total adapter storage grows with the pool, and nearest-prototype search still depends on pool size. The very small reported routing cost is amortized over batches, not proven for arbitrary single-event streaming. Online results omit multiple-seed uncertainty. Treat this as a promising modular design, with capacity and distribution-shift failure modes still needing stress tests.

episodes.title: Understanding Everyday Communication Patterns, Stress, and Productivity in Hybrid Work through Egocentric Wearable Audio Sensing
episodes.headline: Rich training signals, restricted sensing
episodes.description: A wearable audio study distills speaker detection into restricted acoustic features and studies workplace associations.
episodes.takeaway: Separate training-time information from what a deployed sensor retains.
episodes.caveat: Only sixteen employees were analyzed; stress associations are not causal or diagnostic, and feature retention is not a formal privacy guarantee.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.37270v1

episodes.transcript:
Understanding Everyday Communication Patterns, Stress, and Productivity in Hybrid Work through Egocentric Wearable Audio Sensing
First publication: 2026-10-27 | Version: v1 (2026-10-27)
Video produced: 2026-11-01 | Selection digest: 2026-10-30
Publication status: arXiv preprint; peer review not independently verified.
Primary source: https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.37270v1

Can an always-on sensor reveal how office and home communication relate to stress without retaining raw speech? Feng and colleagues study this with a wearable audio badge. Their target is the wearer's speaking time and vocal activeness, not transcription or clinical diagnosis. The difficult part is separating the wearer from nearby voices using deliberately impoverished acoustic features.

The badge samples twenty seconds each minute and immediately extracts pitch, loudness, and twelve coefficients describing the sound spectrum. Keeping these features instead of recordings reduces the information retained, but does not establish formal privacy. The system combines on-device feature extraction with offline speaker analysis; it is not an entirely on-device intelligent agent. Sparse sampling also means communication is estimated rather than continuously observed.

The practical application is longitudinal workplace research. The authors recruited nineteen employees and analyzed sixteen who wore the badge for more than ten days. Each person participated for four months, averaging about forty recorded workdays. Because private workplace speech could not supply labeled training recordings, the speaker detector was trained on three public conversation datasets. This creates a transfer problem: those datasets use smart glasses or meeting microphones, not the deployed badge.

A large speech model first learns to classify each frame as wearer speech, other speech, or silence. Its predictions then supervise a smaller residual convolutional network that receives only the retained spectral coefficients. The large teacher is frozen; the student is updated to match both the labels and the teacher's probability distribution. This is knowledge distillation. At deployment only the student is used offline. Detected wearer frames yield speaking minutes per hour; pitch and loudness relative to each person's distribution yield activeness.

Diarization error measures incorrect speech timing or speaker assignment. On the three public datasets, distillation reduces that error from sixteen to fourteen point one percent, twenty-four point six to twenty-three point five, and thirty-one point eight to twenty-nine. These are modest, consistent improvements, not near-perfect sensing. In the deployment, higher office speaking load is associated with higher self-reported stress and lower productivity after modeled covariates. Those associations do not show that speaking causes either outcome.

For wearable sensing, the reusable idea is separating a rich training-time teacher from a restricted sensing pipeline. But the deployment is a small cohort from one institution, with no external replication. Public training splits include session-level separation, which does not by itself guarantee unseen speakers. Personalized activeness uses a participant's empirical distribution rather than a proven prospective calibration rule. Mixed-effects models account for repeated observations, but neither many surveys nor months of data turn sixteen people into a large independent sample.

episodes.title: TAO: Tool-Aware Joint Scheduling for LLM-Based Agentic Serving
episodes.headline: Schedule the next useful model turn
episodes.description: Tool readiness and decayed inference-cache credit guide joint admission and placement for agent-serving requests.
episodes.takeaway: Separate scheduling value from placement optimization and evaluate complete workload tradeoffs.
episodes.caveat: Gains vary by workload; TAO is worse than ThunderAgent on the reported AutomationBench 128-worker setting. Inference caching is not learned long-term memory.
episodes.source_credit:
arXiv:2610.37230v1
https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.37230v1
arXiv version 2026-10-27
Li et al., original figures and selected table columns, CC BY 4.0 https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/. Cropped and rearranged for readability, experimental values unchanged.
episodes.transcript:
TAO: Tool-Aware Joint Scheduling for LLM-Based Agentic Serving
First publication: 2026-10-27 | Version: v1 (2026-10-27)
Video produced: 2026-11-01 | Selection digest: 2026-10-30
Publication status: arXiv preprint; peer review not independently verified.
Primary source: https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.37230v1

An agent alternates between generating tokens and waiting for tools. A graphics processor cannot accelerate a shell command that is still running elsewhere. Meanwhile, the model's cached attention keys and values may occupy scarce memory. TAO asks which waiting sessions should return to which inference node, and when. This is a serving-system paper, not a new language model, and it does not train the model to reason better.

A session that returns to the same node may reuse its conversation prefix and avoid recomputing it. But cached state can disappear while the tool runs. Admitting one large session also changes which combinations of other sessions fit. Independently choosing the apparently best node for each request can therefore waste capacity. The authors target clustered inference processors with tools executing on separate CPUs, a useful setting for coding and other tool-using agents.

The comparison includes round-robin and cache-aware routing in vLLM, NVIDIA's Dynamo, and ThunderAgent, which interrupts sessions at tool boundaries and uses a packing heuristic. TAO retains that interruption-and-waiting-pool idea. Its addition is to value cached context and imminent tool returns together, then choose a joint placement. These are the authors' evaluated baselines; the paper does not establish an independently verified universal state of the art.

For every session and candidate node, the scheduler builds three ordered quantities. First is reusable cache credit, discounted with a ten-second half-life. Second is whether the tool has finished or is expected within a one-second horizon, using runtime hints and historical durations. Third is token count. The planner maximizes the summed quantities lexicographically: cache credit takes precedence, then readiness breaks ties, then token count. A capacity-state dynamic program considers admitting or skipping each session and assigning admitted sessions to nodes. It is exact only for the frozen, discretized scheduling problem. An asynchronous worker computes the plan, and the executor rechecks live capacity before applying it. Model weights do not change.

On SWE-Lite software tasks with DeepSeek-V4 Flash, two nodes of four H100 processors each, and sixty-four workers, mean end-to-end task latency falls from the best baseline's 253.228 seconds to 185.410. That is 26.8 percent lower. Decode throughput rises from 1561.307 to 2021.523 tokens per second. But gains are workload dependent. On AutomationBench at 128 workers, TAO is worse than ThunderAgent on latency, first-token delay, and throughput. This counterexample matters more than treating the abstract's best-case percentages as a general guarantee.

The reusable idea is to separate session valuation from a joint placement solver, while making external-tool readiness observable. For an always-on agent service this could reduce waste without changing its learned policy, but that transfer is speculative. Cache-age tuning, prediction errors, and the state space of the placement solver remain practical constraints. The authors report planner work below 0.12 percent of runtime in their four-replica sweep. These are author-reported measurements, not an independent reproduction, and lower serving latency should not be confused with improved task accuracy.

episodes.title: SWIM: Learning What Matters from Behaviors for JEPA World Models
episodes.headline: Learn which state changes matter for planning
episodes.description: Behavior-prediction gates shape the distance learned by a visual latent world model.
episodes.takeaway: Use behavior to weight representation distances, while testing policy-dependent shortcuts.
episodes.caveat: Training requires simulator states and logged actions. Default-setting average gains are about one percentage point; no physical-robot transfer is demonstrated.
episodes.source_credit:
arXiv:2610.36662v1 · 27 Oct 2026
https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.36662v1
arXiv preprint v1; venue status documented in companion
Original explanatory diagrams and factual readouts adapted from Hu et al., arXiv:2610.36662v1. Original arXiv nonexclusive distribution license does not establish broad figure reuse; adaptations are labeled and not experimental outputs.
episodes.transcript:
SWIM: Learning What Matters from Behaviors for JEPA World Models
First publication: 2026-10-27 | Version: v1 (2026-10-27)
Video produced: 2026-11-01 | Selection digest: 2026-10-30
Publication status: arXiv preprint; peer review not independently verified.
Primary source: https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.36662v1

A robot planner searches for actions that move its imagined future toward a goal. If distance in the model's representation emphasizes irrelevant visual differences, that search can fail even when prediction looks plausible. A joint-embedding predictive architecture learns to predict future feature vectors rather than reconstruct pixels. This paper asks how to make distances between those vectors reflect the physical changes that actually matter for behavior.

Simulator states can supervise the representation, but equal weighting is not automatically neutral. Repeated encodings of the same variable can count one physical change several times. Irrelevant coordinates can dominate useful ones. Hand-selecting state features is brittle. The proposed alternative learns one importance weight per state coordinate from recorded behavior, without reward labels. Its assumption is that variables useful for explaining actions are also useful for planning; that is plausible, not guaranteed.

The experiments use five visual manipulation tasks from OGBench, a benchmark of offline goal-reaching environments. These include moving one to four cubes and interacting with a scene. The main comparison adds learned weights to the same state-supervised latent world model used by a uniform-weight baseline called SCALE-All. Both receive the same offline trajectories and planning protocol. This isolates weighting more cleanly than comparing unrelated pretrained models. Physical robot deployment is not demonstrated.

First, a small neural network receives the current simulator state and a weighted difference between current and later states. It predicts the action chunk recorded in that trajectory. Trainable sigmoid gates control each displacement coordinate. The loss rewards accurate action prediction, favors the true future over mismatched futures, and penalizes large gate weights. Then the gates are frozen. A second training stage makes distances between image features correlate with distances between weighted states, while retaining future-feature prediction and a non-collapse regularizer. At deployment only images, latent dynamics and action search remain. The state-weighting network is discarded.

The headline table tunes the sparsity weight separately for each task. Under that condition, scene success reaches thirty-nine point four percent, versus thirty-three point four for uniform weights, across five training seeds. That is a six-point gain, not the fixed-setting average gain. With default settings averaged across tasks and both planners, the reported improvements are about one percentage point. A pretrained visual-feature baseline remains better on the three-cube task. These are simulation results from the authors, not a general ranking of world models.

The reusable idea is to shape a representation's distance using what predicts behavior, rather than reconstructing everything equally. For sensing representations, that suggests a hypothesis, not evidence of transfer: weigh changes by their relevance to a downstream decision. The method needs privileged state and logged actions during training. Learned gates can reflect behavior-policy correlations, not causal importance. Mismatched futures are not guaranteed to be impossible alternatives. There is no proof that a global gate vector will remain appropriate when tasks or the policy change.

episodes.title: Proactive Memory for Event-Driven LLM Agents
episodes.headline: Validate a routine before interrupting
episodes.description: An event-driven memory system links summaries to evidence, validates recurring patterns and suppresses duplicate interventions.
episodes.takeaway: Make memory auditable: validate, retrieve, weaken and retire proposed regularities.
episodes.caveat: The small jointly developed benchmark is label-sensitive; home precision is below fifty percent, with no prospective user-benefit trial.
episodes.source_credit:
arXiv:2610.36967v1 · 27 Oct 2026
https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.36967v1
arXiv preprint v1; venue status documented in companion
Original explanatory diagrams and factual readouts adapted from Li et al., arXiv:2610.36967v1. No original figure copied; adaptations are labeled, not experimental outputs.
episodes.transcript:
Proactive Memory for Event-Driven LLM Agents
First publication: 2026-10-27 | Version: v1 (2026-10-27)
Video produced: 2026-11-01 | Selection digest: 2026-10-30
Publication status: arXiv preprint; peer review not independently verified.
Primary source: https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.36967v1

An always-on assistant needs to decide whether a new event warrants help or silence. The useful clue may be a recurring pattern, an unresolved earlier need, or a change that makes an old opportunity actionable again. Simply retrieving similar text does not establish that a pattern is reliable or still relevant. Proactive Memory separates remembering an event from validating a regularity and deciding whether to interrupt.

A summary can invent a detail; repeated summaries can turn it into a false habit. Conversely, a genuine routine can stop being true. Repeated alerts can also be intrusive even when their underlying facts are correct. The method therefore checks summary facts against their original observations, tests proposed patterns against historical records, and tracks what assistance has already been proposed. These controls reduce some errors but do not establish user benefit or permission to act.

The authors introduce ProactiveStream with four thousand five hundred thirty-nine events across seventeen isolated streams. Nine participants provide activity contexts, four homes provide ambient sensor records, and four repositories provide software events. Three annotators adjudicate opportunities for low-risk assistance. Each system starts empty and processes events chronologically. A decision is finalized before its event enters memory; labels are joined only afterward. These are annotated opportunity-detection tests, not clinical outcomes or a prospective user trial.

The recent buffer holds at most ninety-nine prior events within seventy-two hours, plus the current event. At each local day's end, a language model constructs summaries with typed facts and source links; a validator rejects unsupported facts. After seven daily records, it proposes a trigger, expected behavior and time window. Replay requires three supporting days, successful matches on at least half of observable triggered days, and behavior at least as frequent after the trigger as its comparable baseline. These are confidence and lift tests. Current conditions retrieve applicable patterns. Violations weaken or suspend them. Duplicate control suppresses unchanged interventions. Memory and service state change, not model weights.

With the shared Luna language model, overall opportunity-detection F one is fifty-two point six percent, a reported twenty-one point four percent relative improvement over the strongest external baseline. F one balances precision and recall; it is not task success. For home events, precision is forty-eight point six percent and recall seventy-three point seven percent. Thus more than half of interventions still miss the reference opportunity label. Removing replay validation reduces home F one from fifty-eight point six to fifty-four point four. Reference relabeling also changes absolute scores materially.

The reusable contribution is an auditable memory lifecycle: retain evidence, validate a proposed regularity, match it to the present, and retire it when observations contradict it. It is relevant to always-on sensing agents, but the benchmark is small, jointly developed with the method, and label-sensitive. Home coverage spans only fourteen days per home. There is no external prospective validation, patient-level diagnostic task, or proof of improved wellbeing. Deployment would additionally need consent, privacy controls and an explicit boundary between suggesting assistance and performing it.

episodes.title: TransECG-SSL: Hybrid Self-Supervised Representation Learning for ECG Arrhythmia Classification
episodes.headline: Test transfer on unseen patients
episodes.description: Patient-disjoint ECG experiments compare masked reconstruction and contrastive learning with matched encoder baselines.
episodes.takeaway: Frozen cross-database transfer and minority-class metrics make representation claims more interpretable.
episodes.caveat: The hybrid objective does not win every route. Three retrospective datasets, one patient partition and annotated beat centers do not establish clinical readiness.
episodes.source_credit:

https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.35378v1
arXiv preprint; submitted to IEEE JBHI, not accepted
arXiv non-exclusive license does not grant general open reuse. Limited attributed original figure/table excerpts for technical criticism and commentary. Rearranged selections clearly labeled.
episodes.transcript:
TransECG-SSL: Hybrid Self-Supervised Representation Learning for ECG Arrhythmia Classification
First publication: 2026-10-26 | Version: v1 (2026-10-26)
Video produced: 2026-11-01 | Selection digest: 2026-10-30
Publication status: arXiv preprint; peer review not independently verified.
Primary source: https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.35378v1

An electrocardiogram records the heart's electrical activity. A classifier can recognize familiar patients rather than transferable rhythm patterns if their heartbeats appear in both training and testing. TransECG-SSL asks a stricter question: can a representation learned without labels in one database support classification in another, while keeping test patients separate? It is a controlled representation experiment, not a clinically validated diagnostic system.

Normal beats dominate these databases. Always predicting normal already gives roughly eighty-five to eighty-nine percent accuracy on the test sets. Balanced accuracy instead averages recall across heartbeat classes, giving rare classes equal weight. The paper separates patients before training: forty-seven in MIT-BIH, thirty-two in INCART, and seventy-eight in the supraventricular database. Hundreds of thousands of beats do not constitute hundreds of thousands of independent patients.

The plausible use is label-efficient adaptation to a new recording population. Here a lightweight classifier still needs labeled target patients; this is not zero-shot transfer. The authors compare reconstruction, contrastive learning, supervised source training, and an untrained encoder using the same Transformer architecture. That makes objective comparisons more interpretable than comparing unrelated published headline scores. It does not independently establish the current state of the art.

Each input is a one-second, single-lead heartbeat centered on an annotated R peak, the prominent electrical spike. A convolutional front end and four Transformer layers produce a 128-number representation. One training branch hides contiguous signal blocks and reconstructs the missing samples. Another brings representations of the same beat closer after weak noise and amplitude changes, relative to other beats. Both update the encoder. After pretraining, auxiliary heads are discarded and the encoder is frozen. Only a linear target classifier is trained.

The hybrid beats the matched source-supervised encoder in balanced accuracy on all seven routes, but not consistently in macro F1, which balances precision and recall for each class. Reconstruction alone beats the hybrid on three of seven balanced-accuracy comparisons. For INCART to MIT-BIH transfer, the hybrid reaches fifty-five point one percent balanced accuracy, versus fifty-one point eight for reconstruction and forty-two point eight for supervised source training. The contrastive component is useful in some routes, not universally.

The reusable contribution is the evaluation discipline: frozen transfer, architecture-matched baselines, patient-disjoint partitions, and explicit minority-class metrics. For sensing representations, these controls are as important as a new loss. Limitations include one fixed patient partition across five random seeds, annotated beat centers, and three retrospective datasets. INCART has only two test beats in its rarest class. No prospective clinical deployment is demonstrated, and improvements under this training budget do not establish universal superiority of hybrid self-supervision.

episodes.title: Normative Deviation Modeling for EEG-based Depression Detection
episodes.headline: Measure deviation without calling it diagnosis
episodes.description: Healthy-reference reconstruction and denoising residuals supplement EEG representations for retrospective depression classification.
episodes.takeaway: Test whether reference residuals identify the condition or merely acquisition shift.
episodes.caveat: Only two small cohorts are studied. Reverse-transfer calibration uses known healthy target groups, so directional results are not a matched head-to-head comparison.
episodes.source_credit:

https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.37338v1
arXiv preprint; WWW 2027 template does not establish acceptance
arXiv non-exclusive license does not grant general open reuse. Limited attributed original figure/table excerpts for technical criticism and commentary. Rearranged selections clearly labeled.
episodes.transcript:
Normative Deviation Modeling for EEG-based Depression Detection
First publication: 2026-10-27 | Version: v1 (2026-10-27)
Video produced: 2026-11-01 | Selection digest: 2026-10-30
Publication status: arXiv preprint; peer review not independently verified.
Primary source: https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.37338v1

Can deviations from a learned healthy brain-signal reference help a classifier transfer between datasets? Jiang and colleagues investigate this for major depressive disorder using electroencephalography, or EEG, which records scalp electrical activity. Their models distinguish labeled depression and healthy-control recordings. The important distinction is that this is retrospective classification, not evidence that EEG alone can diagnose depression in routine care.

Brain signals vary across people, electrodes, and recording conditions. A classifier may learn those differences instead of depression-related structure. The study uses two public datasets: Mumtaz2016 has sixty-four people, and MODMA has fifty-three. Signals are mapped to nineteen electrode locations and split into overlapping five-second windows. All windows from a person remain together in within-source cross-validation, preventing simple subject leakage. Thousands of windows still represent only these small cohorts.

The proposed use is a representation aid for future screening research. Conventional models learn directly from diagnostic labels; augmentation methods generate extra training examples. Here, generative models instead define what healthy training data look like. This is a useful change of role, but a reconstruction error can reflect an unfamiliar device or artifact as well as pathology. Healthy-reference modeling is not automatically disease-specific or clinically interpretable.

One reference compresses healthy inputs into a learned dictionary and reconstructs them. A second learns to remove added noise from healthy inputs. Reconstruction and denoising errors then measure deviation from those references. The scalar version combines errors into a score and fuses it with a frozen EEG encoder's features. The feature version retains individual residuals from handcrafted signal features and learns attention-based aggregation across windows. Reference models remain frozen while the downstream fusion and classifier learn depression labels. These are the scalar and feature-level normative-deviation methods.

For Mumtaz-to-MODMA transfer, the scalar method reports seventy-eight point five percent accuracy without target calibration. In reverse transfer, the feature method reports eighty-nine point one five percent, but uses seven known healthy target record groups for score calibration. Those groups are excluded from diagnostic testing. The two numbers are not a controlled head-to-head comparison: direction, aggregation, and target access differ. The feature method's reverse-transfer accuracy exceeds the strongest reported baseline by five point four three percentage points.

The reusable idea for sensing is to supplement an embedding with explicit residuals against a reference distribution. Before adopting it, test whether those residuals detect acquisition shift rather than the phenomenon of interest. Reverse-transfer runs reuse overlapping test groups, so repeated runs are not independent cohorts. Only two small datasets are studied, with no prospective clinical utility or broader population validation. The conference template is not acceptance evidence; treat this as an October twenty-seventh preprint, not a validated diagnostic tool.

episodes.description: A geometry turntable conditions multi-view subject-to-video generation without forced alignment to the output trajectory.
episodes.takeaway: Train with deployment-like reconstruction errors and structured geometry context.
episodes.caveat: Aligned point-cloud metrics are not metric-scale reconstruction accuracy. Aesthetic scores trail all listed baselines; rigid objects and small evaluations limit generality.

episodes.transcript:
OmniShowcase: Omnidirectional Subject-Consistent Video Generation from Multi-View Images
First publication: 2026-10-26 | Version: v1 (2026-10-26)
Video produced: 2026-11-01 | Selection digest: 2026-10-30
Publication status: arXiv preprint; peer review not independently verified.
Primary source: https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.35684v1

Given four photographs of an object, generate a video that moves around it without changing its identity or shape. A convincing first frame is not enough: the back of a teapot should remain the back of that same teapot. OmniShowcase tackles this subject-to-video problem by supplying explicit geometry and training on camera motion around real three-dimensional assets. The pictures shown here are the authors' generated examples, not physical reconstructions verified by us.

Multiple reference images reveal more surfaces, but do not explicitly tell a video generator how those views connect in three dimensions. Training videos generated from one image can themselves contain changing geometry. Potential applications include product visualization and controlled synthetic data, although downstream perception benefits are not tested. The paper focuses on objects that remain rigid across the reference views, rather than arbitrary moving people or deforming objects.

Single-view video methods rely heavily on learned appearance priors. Multi-view methods provide additional images, while subject-specific tuning spends optimization on each new object. OmniShowcase instead constructs Showcase-4K, four thousand training videos. A renderer moves a camera around one fixed mesh. Video inpainting generates the background while preserving rendered subject pixels. Four reference views then feed a reconstruction model. This deliberate reconstruction step, rather than using the perfect source mesh as the condition, matches the imperfect geometry available at deployment.

From the reconstructed object, the system renders twenty-five surface-normal maps: images whose colors encode the directions surfaces face. The video model receives four reference images, that fixed turntable, and text describing the desired camera motion. The normal sequence need not align frame by frame with the output. Reference and normal latents remain clean; only target-video latents are mixed with noise. The transformer learns to predict the target's flow from noise toward video. Small low-rank weight updates are trained in the Wan2.1 image-to-video model while its base weights stay frozen. At inference the same reconstruction-and-conditioning pipeline generates a new object video without per-subject optimization.

The held-out benchmark contains fifty subjects with no shared training assets; the real-object NAVI evaluation contains thirty-five subjects. All compared methods receive the same four views. On the held-out set, normalized aligned point-cloud distance falls from the best baseline's 0.1717 to 0.0824. On NAVI it falls from 0.1816 to 0.0975. Lower means the reconstructed generated orbit is closer to reference geometry, after normalization and alignment; it is not a metric-scale reconstruction error. Identity metrics also improve, but the aesthetic score is lower than every listed baseline on both sets.

The interesting reusable principle is to condition generation on a structured physical cue without forcing that cue to follow the output's timeline. This might inform world-model representation design, but planning and action prediction are not demonstrated. Training still took about fifty hours on four B200 processors. Synthetic-looking backgrounds and non-rigid reference subjects remain limitations. When inspected on October thirtieth, the repository advertised a pending release rather than a complete reproducible implementation. The results are author reported, and stronger benchmark scores do not by themselves establish geometrically faithful video in unrestricted real scenes.

episodes.title: Efficient Streaming Audio-Visual Target Speaker Extraction for Real-World Acoustic Scenes
episodes.headline: Extract a voice, then measure the right latency
episodes.description: Visual mouth cues and multiscale audio processing extract a target speaker, with a training-only interference penalty.
episodes.takeaway: Distinguish clip forward-pass cost from streaming buffers and end-to-end delay.
episodes.caveat: The reported 51.3 milliseconds is for a two-second clip, not streaming latency. Real-world evaluation includes ten participants and is not a clinical hearing-assistance trial.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.32749v1
arXiv version 2026-10-23

episodes.transcript:
Efficient Streaming Audio-Visual Target Speaker Extraction for Real-World Acoustic Scenes
First publication: 2026-10-23 | Version: v1 (2026-10-23)
Video produced: 2026-11-01 | Selection digest: 2026-10-30
Publication status: arXiv preprint; peer review not independently verified.
Primary source: https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.32749v1

Falcon extracts one person's voice from overlapping speech using a microphone mixture and a video of that person's mouth. The visual stream identifies whom to listen to. The output is an estimated speech waveform, not a transcript. This matters for conferencing and potentially hearing assistance, but the paper evaluates speech extraction, not clinical hearing outcomes. Its central question is whether realistic acoustic training and a compact separator can improve quality without excessive computation.

Standard mixtures often contain exactly two speakers. Real scenes contain variable numbers of nearby talkers, distant voices, echoes, ambient noise, and abrupt sounds. RealSSA-Sim combines these factors in about 153 hours of simulated audio-visual mixtures. RealSSA-Real is a separate recorded evaluation set: approximately eighty-four minutes, ten participants, and eight environments. It is never used for training or validation. That is useful distribution-shift evidence, but still a small population and environment sample.

Large time-frequency separators can be expensive. Compact methods such as Swift-Net repeatedly apply a small separation block, trading fewer parameters for repeated computation. Falcon uses an encoder-decoder that reduces resolution, collects coarse scene context, then restores detail at several scales in one pass per block. The audio representation is refined before fusion and again after adding mouth-video features. So single-pass does not mean the whole system contains only one block or has zero buffering.

A frozen visual backbone extracts mouth features. An audio encoder represents the mixture across time and frequency. Recurrent layers and masked attention process those features, while the fused visual cue guides a complex-valued mask that reconstructs target speech. During training, the estimated target's embedding is pulled toward the clean target and pushed away from nearby interfering speakers. Reference embeddings use stopped gradients; the estimated-output path still updates the shared encoder and separator. This extra contrastive objective is combined with waveform reconstruction and removed at inference. It needs separate source waveforms, which simulation supplies but ordinary real recordings do not.

On RealSSA-Sim, scale-invariant signal-to-noise improvement is 7.7 decibels, versus 7.6 for the evaluated causal AV-TF-GridNet baseline. Higher means better separation relative to the mixture. Falcon uses 0.5 million trainable parameters versus 6.2 million, and 10.6 billion multiply-accumulate operations versus 213.8 billion. For a two-second input on an RTX 3090, median forward-pass time is 51.3 milliseconds versus 567.8. Crucially, this is not end-to-end streaming delay: the visual branch buffers 120 milliseconds of future frames, and real streaming scheduling overhead still needs measurement.

The added training loss raises Falcon's separation score from 7.3 to 7.7 decibels without an inference branch. Yet real-recording word error rate remains 32.74 percent and is second-best among the compared extractors. The method is single-channel and depends on visible, aligned mouth information. For always-on multimodal systems, the reusable idea is targeted acoustic supervision and careful separation of model compute from sensor latency. Integration into wearables is plausible, not demonstrated. Paper and project page label NeurIPS 2026; this briefing uses the verified October twenty-third arXiv version, without independently confirming proceedings acceptance.

episodes.headline: Must-read: trained read/write memory changes per-conversation state without retraining the backbone
episodes.description: Must-read: trained read/write memory changes per-conversation state without retraining the backbone; compare compression against recall fidelity.
episodes.takeaway: Token-level updates and response training matter more than branding.
episodes.caveat: The most useful ablation replaces token-level writes with one turn-level update: Nano’s average falls from forty-seven to forty-one. episodes.transcript:
MemT-1.0: Towards Memory-Native Evolution

A long-running assistant needs history, but rereading every message is expensive. MemT asks whether a language model can instead carry a compact state that influences later answers. The important trade-off is not simply memory versus no memory. A growing text archive preserves explicit evidence. A fixed-size state compresses that evidence, so details can overwrite one another. This October twentieth revision presents a learned memory mechanism, not proof that an agent autonomously improves its general skills forever.

The demonstrated uses include conversation recall, personalized questions and software agents using prior procedural experience. Ordinary retrieval searches stored records and places selected text in the prompt. Another approach fits small auxiliary weight matrices to each history, paying an optimization cost. MemT learns how to store and read information in advance, then changes a separate state during interaction. This distinction is relevant to continual-memory research. It has not been validated on wearable sensors, and it does not remove the need for an auditable source record.

At selected model layers, current token representations query a persistent matrix. The resulting readout is gated and added to normal attention. After a turn finishes, the input and response produce keys, values and learned erase, write and forget controls. These update the matrix token by token. This is the operational role of the Gated DeltaNet-based update. A new independent conversation starts with zero state. Multiple storage experts expand capacity, but all participate: this is dense memory routing, not sparse computation. During inference, neither the backbone nor the learned read and write weights are retrained.

Training first predicts later tokens from a short current segment plus memory of earlier segments. Then a frozen teacher reads the full history, while the student receives that history only through memory. The memory parameters learn to match the teacher’s next-token probabilities. That is context distillation in concrete terms. The report uses thirty-four billion training tokens. Across eleven memory benchmarks, the larger Flash model averages fifty point six and the smaller Nano model forty-seven, ahead of the strongest listed parametric baseline at thirty-eight point one. But stronger textual-memory systems remain substantially ahead. Different backbones also limit architecture-only conclusions.

At one hundred twenty-eight thousand history tokens, the Nano model reports a one point eight six times end-to-end speedup over cached full context. The experiment uses batch one, two GPUs and a fixed one hundred twenty-eight-token response. Short histories are slower. The reported sixty-six times storage reduction counts per-conversation state, excluding shared model and memory weights. It is not total GPU memory. When experience is inserted during execution, on five hundred SWE-bench Verified software-repair tasks averaged over three runs per task, native memory improves mean success from sixty-six point zero seven to sixty-nine point seven three percent, but only slightly exceeds textual experience, and does not win every setting.

The most useful ablation replaces token-level writes with one turn-level update: Nano’s average falls from forty-seven to forty-one. Removing response post-training falls further, to thirty-six point three. Changing the exact gated update formula has a much smaller effect. The reusable idea is therefore a learned write-and-read interface, not just a named update rule. For continual agents, test latent state alongside exact retrieval at matched evidence budgets. Measure forgotten details, not only bytes. Fixed state remains lossy, and autonomous experience acquisition and consolidation remain open problems.

episodes.headline: Continual robot RL separates new-task reward learning from old-task action matching, with important growing-memory and cost caveats.
episodes.description: Continual robot RL separates new-task reward learning from old-task action matching, with important growing-memory and cost caveats.
episodes.takeaway: Separate the roles of value transfer and behavioral memory.
episodes.caveat: The hardware stopping rule is nineteen successes in a rolling window of twenty episodes. There is no full hardware baseline sweep, and related assemblies may transfer more readily than unrelated tasks. Resetting the critic modestly worsens performance; updating it on old replay also hurts retention. episodes.transcript:
ACCRUE: Continual Off-Policy Reinforcement Learning for Robot Foundation Models

A robot learns to insert one component, then meets a new assembly. Starting reinforcement learning from scratch wastes useful knowledge. Carrying the learner forward can instead destroy its earlier behavior. ACCRUE separates two goals: transfer a useful starting point for the new task, and preserve previously learned actions. It studies contact-rich assembly with known task boundaries and identities. This is not an agent discovering arbitrary new tasks without supervision, and the retained memory is small per task rather than fixed across an unlimited lifetime.

A robot foundation model already proposes actions from images, joint positions and a language instruction. Earlier off-policy methods attach a smaller learner to improve one task using reusable experience. Continual methods must also decide what survives between tasks. ACCRUE tests simulated assembly and a real robot performing peg, gear and shaped-part insertions. It is relevant to continual reinforcement learning, but it is not direct evidence for wearable adaptation. A useful conceptual connection is preserving behavior without assuming that a newly adapted value estimator remains trustworthy everywhere.

At each stage, the base policy is fine-tuned on demonstrations accumulated so far, then frozen during reinforcement learning. A separate frozen visual encoder supplies consistent observation features. The actor receives those features, joint state and the base model’s proposed action chunk, then refines that chunk. The critic estimates its return. Both small networks carry their trained weights into the next stage. Freezing the observation encoder keeps old replay features compatible even when the base policy changes. The actor is also penalized for straying too far from the base proposal.

Current-task transitions update the critic and train the actor to obtain higher predicted reward. Earlier tasks use a different target. Before new learning begins, the previous actor produces actions for retained historical transitions. Those outputs are cached. The new actor learns to match them, rather than asking its changing critic which old actions are valuable. This is actor distillation: output matching preserves prior behavior. The method keeps the last several episodes from every completed task. Total stored experience therefore grows with the number of tasks.

On the FORGE simulation benchmark, a score averaging new-task learning success and later retained success is point eight six nine, versus point seven one eight for sequential learning and point six nine seven for ordinary replay. Final success is ninety-one point seven percent versus sixty-eight point five and sixty-two point six. These comparisons share the actor–critic setup and aggregate four task orders and four seeds. Real-robot subsequent-task interaction time falls by thirty-one to sixty-eight point five percent. That excludes demonstration collection and total training wall time. Earlier-task evaluations achieve eighteen to twenty successes in twenty trials.

The hardware stopping rule is nineteen successes in a rolling window of twenty episodes. There is no full hardware baseline sweep, and related assemblies may transfer more readily than unrelated tasks. Resetting the critic modestly worsens performance; updating it on old replay also hurts retention. However, the visual-encoder ablation changes both encoder identity and stability, so it cannot isolate representation drift. The key reusable design is to separate current reward learning from prior behavior preservation. Code is marked coming soon. Official footage is linked, not reproduced here.

episodes.caveat: These are supervised readout results, not demonstrated wearable deployment, continual learning or universal planning gains.

episodes.transcript:
Time-JEPA: Grounding Video World Models with Physical Time Series

1 / Problem and central idea
Time-JEPA gives a video model an extra job during training: recover physical measurements at the moment they happened. Those measurements supervise training; evaluation uses video alone. That is the whole mechanism in one sentence. A video can show someone bending a knee, but a useful representation should also preserve how the angle and motion change.

2 / Demonstrated applications
The study covers driving, robot manipulation, and human motion. It tests current physical-state decoding, prediction up to one second ahead, and reconstruction of trajectories or limb distances. Separate tests examine physical anomalies and future object contact. Wearable sensing is a possible extension. The human-motion targets here are pose-derived quantities, not an evaluated wearable inertial-sensor pipeline.

3 / Position among existing methods
The starting point is the released V-JEPA 2.1 video encoder. Physical supervision itself is not new: earlier methods already ground visual representations with physical state. Time-JEPA's distinction is a simple, temporally aligned regression interface across three domains. The strongest comparison is against the same backbone fine-tuned on the same videos without that extra supervision. It is not a universal planning leaderboard result.

4 / Architecture, loss and inference
One branch sees masked video and predicts missing latent features. A slowly updated target encoder supplies the answers. The added branch uses the same online encoder on the full clip. At each temporal position, it averages spatial features and predicts physical quantities through a small head. Measurements are aligned, pooled over adjacent frame pairs, and normalized. Training combines latent prediction with a robust regression loss. After training, discard the auxiliary head, freeze the encoder, and train new task-specific probes, meaning small supervised readout models. Evaluation uses video alone. Variables called out-of-distribution were excluded from encoder supervision, but their probes still receive training labels. This is not zero-shot discovery.

5 / Results and mechanism checks
Against matched video-only fine-tuning, human-motion current-state R-squared, where higher means more variation is explained, rises from 0.231 to 0.345 on seen conditions. For robot manipulation, it rises from 0.424 to 0.725. These are representation-probing results, not task-success rates. With multi-domain training, future-state normalized error under both variable and condition shifts falls from 0.911 to 0.844. Reconstructing human limb distances under held-out conditions reduces mean absolute error from 7.12 to 4.56 centimeters. The crucial ablation changes timing. Correct human-motion alignment gives a correlation of 0.589. A 0.8-second offset gives 0.575. Measurements from another take reduce it to 0.510, barely above the video-only control's 0.503. Local correspondence matters more than simply supplying plausible numbers.

6 / Limits and relevance
There are limits. Physical-anomaly accuracy on GRASP reaches only 57.8 percent, and Physion's all-scenario accuracy is essentially unchanged. Training adds an extra encoder pass, and wearable-device latency is not reported. No continual learning or closed-loop control is demonstrated. For wearable research, the next experiment is synchronized motion supervision, followed by cross-person and device-shift tests and a real downstream decision. That is a proposal, not a demonstrated application. Time-JEPA offers a simple way to make video features more physically informative, with unusually useful synchronization checks.

episodes.transcript:
RL-Guided Temporal Localization for Dual-Channel Retrieval in Long-Horizon Agent Memory

1 / Problem
TIDER tackles a familiar memory error: finding the right topic from the wrong day. Imagine asking about dinner after a family birthday. Semantic search can retrieve several other dinners and miss the one you meant. TIDER first predicts when the evidence should be. A separate temporal retrieval channel then adds memories from those dates, before the answer model sees its context. The key idea is to fix evidence selection, rather than hope the answer model repairs missing evidence.

2 / Applications
The demonstrated application is personal-memory question answering. LifeBench mixes synthetic chats, phone activity, travel, exercise records, and notes. LoCoMo tests long conversations. The authors evaluate separate LifeBench users and transfer the locator to LoCoMo without training on that dataset. Wearable event logs are a plausible extension, but this study does not process raw camera, audio, or motion signals, and it uses no real personal-memory corpus.

3 / Current state of the art
The closest comparisons are temporal memory trees, represented by TiMem, and answer-time temporal reasoning, represented by NeSTR. TIDER reruns these with the same answer-model identity and twenty retrieved memory units. Those units differ in size, so this is not a matched token budget. A September study already learned explicit time intervals for document reranking. TIDER's narrower contribution is reinforcement-trained, potentially multiple windows that generate additional candidates from personal histories. No matched comparison with that study is reported.

4 / Method
Here is the pipeline. An offline process extracts dated events, clusters nearby similar items, and summarizes them. For each question, a Qwen three, one point seven billion parameter locator reads thirty relevant timeline summaries. It predicts a temporal switch and date windows. When the switch is on, overlapping memories join the semantic candidates. Ranking adds an overlap bonus and discounts distant dates, while retaining a floor so distant relevant evidence can survive. The final twenty units go to a fixed answer model. Training begins with supervised examples, then compares eight sampled window outputs and favors the higher-reward choices. Rewards cover detecting temporal need, matching gold windows, retrieving gold evidence, and answering correctly. This uses explicit evidence and date supervision, not just answer rewards.

5 / Results and limitations
On four hundred eight LifeBench questions, TIDER scores sixty-one point five two percent, versus NeSTR's fifty-two point seven zero. On LoCoMo, it reaches seventy-eight point nine six, versus TiMem's seventy-five point three zero. The cleaner ablation holds memory construction fixed: temporal retrieval adds nine point three one percentage points. Reinforcement learning adds five point eight eight points over supervised training alone. But on LoCoMo's temporal questions, TIDER trails TiMem: seventy-one point six five versus seventy-seven point six three. Training takes about one hundred hours on two A one hundred GPUs for one reinforcement-learning run. The temporal pathway adds point four one seconds per query. The gains depend on synthetic histories with comparatively clean dates.

6 / Novelty and relevance
The practical lesson is that a growing memory needs temporal disambiguation as well as semantic similarity. TIDER learns how to read accumulated events; it does not demonstrate continuous online model learning or resistance to forgetting. For wearable-memory research, the useful next test would preserve source identifiers and uncertain event timestamps, then stress repeated activities, missing dates, and clock drift. Keep a semantic fallback when time is unreliable. This paper provides a concrete retrieval mechanism and controlled evidence to investigate that direction, rather than proof of wearable readiness.

episodes.transcript:
BeJEPA: A Goal-Conditioned Humanoid Behavior World Model via Unsupervised RL

1. Problem
BeJEPA chooses a humanoid's action using two predictions: what this action changes next, and what the goal-conditioned policy is expected to achieve afterward. That second prediction summarizes future state features, avoiding a long imagined rollout during policy learning. Why is that useful? A robot can copy a pose while standing in the wrong place. Returning may require a step that temporarily worsens posture matching. The controller must value where that step leads.

2. Applications
The physical Unitree G1 demonstrations show returning after a kick, standing from the ground, and changing goals while retaining a world reference. LiDAR supplies position and heading estimates. These are qualitative demonstrations, not a measured hardware success rate. Simulation evaluates twenty-second motion tracking and fixed goals. Manipulation, wearable sensing, and lifelong adaptation are not demonstrated. Those would require new interfaces and experiments.

3. Current state of the art
The relevant baselines are world-input BFM-Zero, SONIC, and Humanoid-GPT. Their original training scales and objectives differ, so the meaningful numerical comparison is this paper's matched evaluation. BeJEPA improves global alignment, but SONIC still wins AMASS local posture. The closest representation precedent is TD-JEPA, which already learns long-term latent predictions. The new question is whether separating immediate physics from behavioral continuation improves humanoid control.

4. Method
A shared encoder maps posture, position, and heading into 256 dimensions. Dynamic predicts the next latent from the current latent and action. Successor predicts discounted future latents under the goal-conditioned policy. Comparing its output with the goal supplies an action value; gradients through both predictors improve the actor. Dynamic learns from observed next states. Successor uses temporal-difference bootstrapping. Both train the representation, emphasizing physical prediction early. Motion priors and physical penalties also guide behavior. A history encoder consumes deployable observations and supplies a latent. At inference, optional model-predictive control corrects the actor using frozen dynamics. Balanced refinement looks sixteen steps ahead and optimizes eight action residuals, then replans. It activates only on slower reference segments.

5. Results
On AMASS, balanced BeJEPA-MPC reaches 219.5 millimetres of global joint-position error, versus 573.4 for world-input BFM-Zero and 531.5 for SONIC: reductions of 61.7 and 58.7 percent. Local posture favors SONIC: 49.7 versus 63.9 millimetres. In the fixed-goal ablation, full BeJEPA's mean position error is 0.642 metres, versus 1.348 for a comparable-capacity merged predictor. Blocking either predictor's representation gradient also hurts. Balanced refinement reduces AMASS tracking lag from 94.8 to 21.2 milliseconds. The tracking tables omit confidence intervals, seed counts, and a precise test-segment list.

6. Novelty and relevance
The contribution is joint learning of local physical prediction and goal-conditioned continuation. For world models, that is a useful design pattern. But uncorrected dynamics drift at longer horizons. Actor plus history encoder total 33 million parameters; all online training networks total 394 million. Training GPU-hours and measured MPC latency are unreported. For continual memory or wearables, relevance is indirect: no episodic recall, no deployment weight learning, and roughly a one-second discount scale. The official demo is live; code is promised before mid-November.

episodes.transcript:
ECG-SDI: Single-lead Electrocardiogram Enables Continuous Sleep Depth Index Profiling and Scalable Digital Biomarkers for Sleep Health

1. Problem and assumptions
ECG-SDI asks whether one electrical heart-signal lead, or ECG, can produce a continuously varying sleep-depth score, rather than only five stage labels. Its central move is ordinal learning: teach the score that waking is shallower than N1, then N2, then N3. Rapid-eye-movement sleep, or REM, gets a separate classifier because it does not fit that ordering. This assumes cardiac physiology carries useful depth information. The target remains conventional sleep staging, not independently measured continuous depth. This is an October sixteenth preprint.

2. Demonstrated applications
The authors study overnight trajectories, sleep phenotypes and changes around positive-airway-pressure treatment, or CPAP. Their twelve thousand three hundred ninety-two recordings include ten thousand six hundred fifty-two development recordings, seven hundred twenty-six external Cleveland participants, and two nights each from five hundred seven CPAP participants. Recordings are not independent people. Development splits are participant-level. These are retrospective sleep-study cohorts; the wearable demonstration illustrates a workflow, rather than validating home accuracy or treatment decisions.

3. Current research context
Continuous sleep depth is not new. The same group's April 2025 study used EEG, eye movements, muscle activity and ECG with an ordinal objective. March 2026's Holter-to-Sleep supplied an ECG staging backbone. ECG-SDI combines that narrower sensing input with depth ranking and treatment-associated analyses. There is no matched benchmark showing superiority to an EEG-derived continuous-depth index. Its contribution is an accessible sensing direction and cohort analysis, not an established new gold standard.

4. Concrete method
Thirty-second ECG segments are combined with thirty-nine spectral and wavelet features. A convolutional encoder creates each representation. Fifteen-epoch windows feed a Transformer that also sees recording-level context, so this is offline processing. After sleep-stage pretraining, the backbone is frozen. Two residual heads learn REM classification and a scalar depth. Training adds REM cross-entropy to half-weighted pairwise ranking, excluding REM and equal-stage pairs. A crucial dependency follows: the displayed zero-to-one score uses each recording's reference Wake and non-REM labels to choose normalization percentiles. Several reported biomarkers also require reference stages.

5. Results and evidence strength
Raw depth correlates with ordered Wake and non-REM stages at point eight two eight internally and point eight four eight in Cleveland. The CPAP cohort is harder: point four five six before treatment and point five four six afterward. These are stage-agreement results, not continuous-depth accuracy. In the paired analysis, normalized depth area rises six point one percent and shallow-sleep burden falls sixteen percent. Those are relative changes in five hundred seven participants without a randomized control. Cardiac effects of treatment could contribute. The very narrow stage-agreement intervals bootstrap epochs, not independent participants.

6. Novelty, limits and wearable relevance
For wearable research, learning from an inexpensive ECG channel is useful. But the normalized outputs are not yet label-free, and older cohorts dominate development; the CPAP group is mostly men with severe apnea. Mortality associations are observational, not validated individual risk predictions. Home accuracy, power and latency are unmeasured. The public repository has no weights or license, limiting reproducibility. I would treat this as a promising research index whose next test needs label-free calibration, participant-level uncertainty and prospective validation across diverse wearable users.

episodes.headline: PulseBound closes a hidden future-data channel before preprocessing
episodes.description: Prefix-only normalization and suffix replacement make future-beat prediction auditable. Matched forecasting and transfer gains come with explicit tokenizer, preprocessing and dataset-split limits.

episodes.transcript:
PulseBound: Future-Beat State Forecasting Under an Explicit Information Boundary

1. Problem and assumptions
PulseBound addresses a subtle forecasting trap: an attention mask that blocks future tokens cannot help if whole-window normalization or a frequency transform already exposes the future. It normalizes only the visible pulse-wave prefix, replaces the hidden suffix before constructing derived views, and aligns their masks. The model then predicts physiological descriptors of up to four future valid beats. The assumption is that these extractor-defined targets teach transferable physiology. First posted October eighth and revised October twelfth, this remains an under-review preprint.

2. Demonstrated applications
The backbone trains on hospital pulse waves from MIMIC and VitalDB, with respectively three hundred fourteen and two hundred ninety-four held-out patient groups. Both sources also contribute training patients, so this is not unseen-source forecasting. Thirteen downstream benchmarks cover vital signs, stress, activity, identity and signal quality. Inference needs only a complete thirty-second pulse-wave window; ECG and other auxiliary signals are training scaffolds. Those demonstrations support representation research, not wrist-device accuracy or clinical diagnosis.

3. Current research context
Recent comparators include AnyPPG, introduced in November 2025 and revised in June 2026, and January 2026's SIGMA-PPG. PulseBound tests seven complete systems using matched downstream examples, outer splits and metrics. It reports the best mean on nine of thirteen frozen-probe tasks and seven after full fine-tuning. For example, stress AUC, measuring ranking discrimination, rises from AnyPPG's point nine one eight to point nine five three. That is a protocol-specific comparison. It does not establish universal leadership or isolate which pretraining component caused the gain.

4. Concrete method
Thirty one-second patches generate raw and paired derived-view tokens, plus twenty learned summary tokens, called registers. A twelve-layer, seven-hundred-sixty-eight-wide Transformer processes them with restricted information flow. A shared head receives prefix context, cutoff information and a horizon embedding. It predicts nine rhythm and morphology descriptors; optional pulse-arrival time comes from ECG during training. The loss combines validity-masked Smooth-L1 state prediction with token classification, waveform reconstruction and auxiliary objectives. A curriculum extends the forecast horizon. No teacher network is needed, but an exponential moving average tracks weights. Downstream inference averages register and temporal features from the full window.

5. Matched results and ablations
Against last-visible-beat persistence, transformed-state error falls twenty-eight point zero six percent on MIMIC and twenty-two point twenty-two percent on VitalDB. These average matched patient-level results across states, cutoffs and horizons; they are not blood-pressure error reductions. The ablation matters: full-model future-state Skill, measuring error improvement over a training-median predictor, is point three nine two six, versus point three five two seven without state supervision, and point zero zero three two with shuffled targets. This supports meaningful target alignment, while the no-state control retains substantial predictive information. Removing individual components does not consistently worsen every transfer task.

6. Novelty, limitations and sensing relevance
Changing stored suffixes produced zero recorded prediction changes in the audit. But the guarantee begins after upstream preprocessing. More importantly, the frozen tokenizer was trained on the full processed MIMIC corpus before the patient split; the whole pipeline is not patient-disjoint. Some downstream datasets also have overlap or split limitations. Ninety-eight million parameters and A100 timing do not demonstrate wearable feasibility. The useful novelty is an auditable information-access contract, with explicit limits. Independent raw-signal audits, genuinely external cohorts and device measurements are the next tests.

episodes.transcript:
Few-Shot Prototype Head Adaptation for On-Device ECG Personalization on PSoC 6

1. Problem and assumptions
This October fifth preprint proposes a simple way to personalize an electrical heart-signal, or ECG, classifier on a microcontroller. Freeze the feature extractor, average a few labeled normal and abnormal beats into two prototypes, then classify new beats by their nearest prototype. It avoids updating convolutional weights or maintaining an optimizer. The key assumption is that a tiny frozen embedding already separates patient-specific morphology. This is useful engineering, but its claim of patient-independent evaluation has a concrete split defect we will examine.

2. Demonstrated applications
The authors run replayed ECG beats on a PSoC six Cortex M4F at one hundred megahertz. Measured computation is eleven point three nine milliseconds per pre-segmented beat, with five point two kilobytes of model flash and twenty-two point two kilobytes of model-and-adaptation RAM at ten shots. These exclude the complete firmware. The system receives annotated R-peak windows; it does not validate an upstream beat detector or a live wearable. The window includes roughly three hundred milliseconds after the peak, beyond the quoted compute time.

3. Current research context
Microcontroller learning already includes sparse gradient methods, such as 2022's On-Device Training Under 256 Kilobytes, and 2024 activity-recognition personalization. Here, the contribution is a smaller ECG adaptation primitive with measured hardware behavior. It is not the first prototype classifier or a matched victory over those different tasks. The relevant comparison is the paper's own frozen linear head, adapted with fifty gradient steps. Even within this study, larger backbones can favor gradient adaptation at low shot counts.

4. Concrete method
Each beat contains two hundred samples at three hundred sixty hertz, normalized separately. Two one-dimensional convolution layers, pooling and a projection produce thirty-two numbers using one thousand three hundred fourteen parameters. Offline supervised training learns the backbone, which stays frozen on the device. For each class, adaptation computes the mean support embedding. Inference chooses the smaller squared Euclidean distance. A restricted mode updates only the normal prototype while keeping the training-set abnormal prototype. It reduces abnormal-label demand, but still assumes the supposedly normal support beats are correctly identified.

5. Matched results and costs
Macro F1 averages class precision-and-recall scores. At one shot, it rises from point six three five to point seven three one. At ten shots, it rises from point six four six to point seven nine seven. Those baselines use their matching eligible subsets; increasing shots also excludes difficult records. On-device replay covers eighteen episodes and five hundred seventy-six queries, matching host prototype F1 exactly at point seven nine eight. The timing distinction matters: one-shot calibration takes twenty-two point eight three milliseconds for prototypes versus twenty-four point four nine for gradient adaptation. The advertised seventeen-fold difference applies to Python-host timing, not the microcontroller.

6. Independent split audit and verdict
Here is the central caveat. The official code places record two hundred one in development and two hundred two in testing. PhysioNet documents that these recordings belong to the same person. That contradicts the repository's patient-disjoint description. We cannot quantify any score inflation without rerunning a corrected split. The study also lacks external validation and uses a small historical arrhythmia dataset. This does not erase the hardware demonstration. It makes the paper a useful personalization prototype whose population-generalization claim needs repair, not a clinically ready monitor.

episodes.transcript:
HexaShell: A Thin Harness for Exploring the Limits of VLM Agents as Robot Coding Agents

1 / Actors and persistent updates
Give a robot a coding agent, three cameras, and a small command interface. When an attempt fails, let another copy of the agent repair the code that caused the failure. Freeze those repairs, and test them on new scenes. That is the experiment in HexaShell, a robotics preprint from Hongcheng Gao and colleagues.

The important detail is where learning happens. The language model's weights stay fixed. What changes is a library of small programs for measuring objects and executing motions. One agent acts. Another reads its logs, diagnoses a failure, edits a tool and runs checks. The repaired tool survives into the next episode.

2 / Pixels to metric motion
The harness translates commands into robot motion. It does not supply a task strategy. The agent sees a head camera, two wrist cameras, camera calibration and the robot's own state. It cannot look up the simulator's hidden object positions.

So how does it turn a pixel into a grasp? A calibrated pixel defines a ray through space. If the target lies on a measured plane, intersect that ray with the plane. If two cameras see the same point, triangulate their rays. When the head view is insufficient, move a wrist camera and measure again. Those viewing motions count against the robot's action budget.

3 / One concrete repair
This sounds classical because the geometry is classical. The contribution is getting an agent to build, debug and reuse it. In one example, a xylophone tool mislocated a held mallet by about twenty-three millimeters. The repair matched a second view and triangulated its center. On the next attempt, the error was 2.7 millimeters and the task succeeded.

4 / Results and sample mismatch
Now the results. Across forty-two simulated RoboDojo tasks, the frozen tools achieve 39.7 percent success using the leaderboard's aggregation formula. The paper compares that with 32.3 percent for the strongest learned-policy entry in its October fourteenth snapshot. That competitor, VPP2, learns a visual planner and an action model from manipulation data.

But these are different evaluation samples. HexaShell tests ten new layouts on one seed per task; leaderboard entries use fifty episodes on each of three seeds. The agent also receives task recipes and tool notes. So this is an encouraging reported comparison, with clear limits on the ranking claim.

5 / Controlled evidence and failures
The cleaner ablation is the geometry choice. On the same development layouts, triangulation scores 38.3 percent versus 29.6 percent for a monocular depth network. It uniquely solves fifty-seven layouts and loses twenty-three. Extra views help, even though moving the cameras consumes steps.

The failures are revealing. Pushing reaches 92.5 percent, while tight insertion reaches only 8.3 percent. Nineteen task variants never succeed. Better scene measurement does not automatically produce the continuous corrections needed when a part contacts a tight opening.

6 / Costs and useful scope
There is a substantial time bill. A typical test episode takes about twelve minutes of wall time for twenty-six seconds of simulated robot motion. The simulator pauses while the model thinks. Development requires hundreds of repair rounds, and some tools descend from earlier depth-based and human-assisted work. The public release includes the tools but omits the full harness.

The demonstrated application is therefore simulated robot-tool development. Real-time physical deployment remains untested. What makes this paper worth watching is the inspectable learning loop: failures become concrete software fixes, and the evaluation shows both where those fixes help and where contact control still defeats them.
